title: Applied Multilevel Modeling in R
text:
Welcome
This is an online companion to EDUS 664, Multilevel Modeling, at Virginia Commonwealth University. Each chapter works through the R code for one module of the course, using the same datasets you will use in your assignments.
The book is meant to sit alongside the lectures and demonstration videos, not to replace them. The videos explain why we do things. These pages show you the code, so that you have something you can copy, adapt, and come back to later.

title: Applied Multilevel Modeling in R
text:
How to use this book
Each chapter follows the same shape. We load the data, look at it before modeling it, fit a series of models that build on one another, and interpret what comes out. Code appears in gray blocks, and you can copy any block by hovering over it and clicking the copy icon in the corner.
You may want to work through a chapter with RStudio open next to your browser, running each block as you go. Reading code is not the same as writing it, and the difference shows up quickly once you start the assignments.

title: Applied Multilevel Modeling in R
text:
Software you will need
You will need R and RStudio, both free. The chapters use a common set of packages, which you can install once:

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",     # data management and graphics
  "haven",         # reading Stata and SPSS files
  "psych",         # descriptive statistics and reliability
  "lme4",          # fitting multilevel models
  "lmerTest",      # tests for random effects
  "performance",   # ICC, R-squared, model checks
  "see",           # required by performance's check_model()
  "broom.mixed",   # tidy model output and residuals
  "modelsummary",  # publication-style results tables
  "ggeffects",     # predicted values and interaction plots
  "nlme",          # alternative variance structures
  "influence.ME",  # Cook's distance for multilevel models
  "clubSandwich"   # cluster-robust standard errors
))

A note on two of these. see is not loaded directly anywhere in this book, but performance::check_model() will not produce its diagnostic plots without it, and the error message when it is missing is not especially clear. influence.ME and clubSandwich are used only in Chapter 10, so you can defer installing them until you get there.
A note on packages that appear in older course materials. Earlier versions of these demonstrations used stargazer for results tables. That package is no longer actively maintained and can fail with current versions of R, so the chapters here use modelsummary instead. If you find stargazer code in an old handout, modelsummary() is the direct replacement.

title: Applied Multilevel Modeling in R
text:
Data
Most chapters use a dataset that is either included with this book or posted on Canvas. Each chapter names its dataset at the top. If you are running the code yourself, keep the data file in the same folder as your Quarto document, so that a plain filename like read_csv("hsbmerged.csv") will find it.

title: Applied Multilevel Modeling in R
text:
A word about interpretation
The code in this book will run. That is the easy part, and it is also the part that matters least. What multilevel modeling asks of you is the ability to say what a variance component means, why a random slope belongs in a model, and what a coefficient does and does not license you to claim. The chapters try to model that kind of reasoning in the prose between the code blocks. That prose is worth reading slowly.

title: 1  Getting Started with R
text:
1.1 Packages
R by itself is fairly minimal. Almost everything we do relies on packages, which are collections of functions other people have written. You install a package once, and then load it in every session where you want to use it.

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "haven", "psych"))


library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(psych)

A habit worth forming immediately: put all of your library() calls at the top of your document, not scattered through it. When you render a Quarto document, R runs it top to bottom in a fresh session, and a package loaded halfway down cannot help the code above it.

title: 1  Getting Started with R
text:
1.2 Reading data in
Which function you use depends on the file format. read_dta(), from the haven package, reads Stata files, which is what most of the course datasets are distributed as. read_csv() handles comma-separated files.

hsb2 <- read_dta("hsb2.dta")

Use a plain filename, not a full path like C:/Users/yourname/Downloads/hsb2.dta. Keeping the data file in the same folder as your document is what allows your code to run on someone else’s computer, which is the whole point of a reproducible analysis.

title: 1  Getting Started with R
section: 1.4 The first real trap: categorical variables stored as numbers
text:
1.4 The first real trap: categorical variables stored as numbers
Look carefully at prog in the output above. describe() happily reports a mean for it, something in the neighborhood of 2. That number is meaningless.
prog is not a quantity. It is a label: 1 for general, 2 for academic, 3 for vocational. The mean of a label tells you nothing, because the distance from general to academic is not a real distance, and “2” is not twice “1” in any sense that matters.
The right descriptive statistic for a variable like this is a count:

table(hsb2$prog)


  1   2   3 
 45 105  50 



# As proportions
prop.table(table(hsb2$prog))


    1     2     3 
0.225 0.525 0.250 


You can check how a variable is stored, and see any labels that came along with the Stata file, using str():

str(hsb2$prog)

 dbl+lbl [1:200] 1, 3, 1, 3, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1...
 @ label       : chr "type of program"
 @ format.stata: chr "%9.0g"
 @ labels      : Named num [1:3] 1 2 3
  ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:3] "general" "academic" "vocation"


This matters enormously later. If you leave a multi-category variable like prog or race coded 1, 2, 3 and drop it into a regression, R will treat it as continuous and estimate a single slope, as though moving from general to academic has the same meaning as moving from academic to vocational. The model will run. The results will be wrong, and no error message will tell you.
The fix is to convert such variables into factors, with labels attached:

hsb2 <- hsb2 |>
  mutate(
    prog_f   = factor(prog, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                      labels = c("General", "Academic", "Vocational")),
    ses_f    = factor(ses, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                      labels = c("Low", "Middle", "High")),
    female_f = factor(female, levels = c(0, 1),
                      labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    schtyp_f = factor(schtyp, levels = c(1, 2),
                      labels = c("Public", "Private"))
  )

table(hsb2$prog_f)


   General   Academic Vocational 
        45        105         50 

table(hsb2$ses_f)


   Low Middle   High 
    47     95     58 








A shortcut for Stata files



Stata files often carry value labels with them. When they do, haven::as_factor() converts a variable to a factor using those labels, saving you from typing them out:
hsb2 <- hsb2 |> mutate(prog_f = as_factor(prog))
Always check the result with table(). If the labels did not come through, fall back to specifying them yourself as above.

title: 1  Getting Started with R
text:
1.5 The pipe
You will see |> throughout this book. It is R’s pipe operator, and it takes whatever is on the left and passes it as the first argument to whatever is on the right. These two lines do the same thing:

describe(hsb2$write)
hsb2$write |> describe()

The pipe becomes worth using when operations chain together. Instead of nesting functions inside one another and reading from the inside out, you read left to right in the order the steps happen.

hsb2 |>
  group_by(ses_f) |>
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean_write = mean(write, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_write = sd(write, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  ses_f      n mean_write sd_write
  <fct>  <int>      <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Low       47       50.6     9.49
2 Middle    95       51.9     9.11
3 High      58       55.9     9.44


You may also see %>% in older code, including some of the course handouts. It is an earlier version of the same idea from the magrittr package, and for our purposes the two behave identically.

title: 1  Getting Started with R
text:
1.6 Graphics
Base R’s hist() is fine for a quick look at one variable:

hist(hsb2$write,
     main = "Distribution of Writing Scores",
     xlab = "Standardized writing score")



Figure 1.1: A quick base R histogram of writing scores.



But ggplot2, part of the tidyverse, is what we will use for anything that needs to be readable by someone else. The logic takes a moment to click. You specify a dataset, then a mapping from variables to visual properties inside aes(), then layers of geometry.

ggplot(hsb2, aes(x = write)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#1a7a6e", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Writing Scores",
    x = "Standardized writing score",
    y = "Number of students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()



Figure 1.2: The same distribution in ggplot2.




1.6.1 Comparing groups, and why the axis scale matters
Suppose you want to compare writing scores across the three SES groups. One approach is to split the data into three pieces and plot each one:

low    <- hsb2 |> filter(ses == 1)
middle <- hsb2 |> filter(ses == 2)
high   <- hsb2 |> filter(ses == 3)

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
hist(low$write,    main = "Low SES",    xlab = "Writing score")
hist(middle$write, main = "Middle SES", xlab = "Writing score")
hist(high$write,   main = "High SES",   xlab = "Writing score")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))



Figure 1.3: Three separately generated histograms. Note that the axes differ.



Look at the horizontal and vertical axes across those three panels. They are not the same, because each plot scaled itself to its own data. Any comparison you make by eye is distorted, and differences can look larger or smaller than they are purely as an artifact of the scaling.
Faceting solves this by drawing one plot split into panels, with shared axes:

ggplot(hsb2, aes(x = write)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#1a7a6e", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ses_f) +
  labs(
    title = "Writing Scores by Socioeconomic Status",
    x = "Standardized writing score",
    y = "Number of students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()



Figure 1.4: Writing scores by SES, on a shared scale.



With only 200 students spread across three groups, histograms are fairly lumpy. Boxplots or density curves often compare distributions more clearly at this sample size:

ggplot(hsb2, aes(x = ses_f, y = write, fill = ses_f)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#e0f2ef", "#8cc9c0", "#1a7a6e")) +
  labs(
    title = "Writing Scores by Socioeconomic Status",
    x = NULL, y = "Standardized writing score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")



Figure 1.5: The same comparison as boxplots.



Notice how much the three groups overlap. There is a difference in the averages, and there is also a great deal of variation within each group. Both facts are true at once, and keeping them both in view is a habit worth building now. Group differences almost never mean that group membership determines an individual outcome.

title: 1  Getting Started with R
section: 1.7 Where to go when something breaks
text:
1.7 Where to go when something breaks
Error messages in R are often unhelpful at first and become readable with practice. A few of the most common:
could not find function "..." almost always means a package is not loaded. Check your library() calls.
object '...' not found means you are referring to something that does not exist in your current session, often because of a typo or because you created it in a chunk that has not been run.
undefined columns selected usually means a variable name is misspelled or capitalized differently than you think. R is case sensitive, and Write is not write.
When you are stuck, ?function_name opens the help page for any function, and the examples at the bottom of those pages are often more useful than the descriptions at the top.

title: 2  Review of Regression
text:
2.1 Preparing the variables
The dummy variables here are coded 1 for yes and 0 for no. Race is coded 1 for White, 2 for Black, and 3 for Other. That coding is a poor measurement approach from a QuantCrit standpoint, collapsing enormously different populations into a residual “other” category, but it was typical of 1988 and it is what the file contains. Keep the limitation in mind when interpreting anything involving race.

nlsw <- nlsw |>
  mutate(
    collgrad_f = factor(collgrad, levels = c(0, 1),
                        labels = c("Not college grad", "College grad")),
    race_f     = factor(race, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
                        labels = c("White", "Black", "Other")),
    union_f    = factor(union, levels = c(0, 1),
                        labels = c("Non-union", "Union"))
  )

table(nlsw$collgrad_f)


Not college grad     College grad 
            1714              532 

table(nlsw$race_f)


White Black Other 
 1637   583    26 



2.1.1 A note on missing data

nlsw |>
  summarize(across(c(wage, age, ttl_exp, collgrad, union, hours, industry),
                   ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  variable n_missing
  <chr>        <int>
1 wage             0
2 age              0
3 ttl_exp          0
4 collgrad         0
5 union          368
6 hours            4
7 industry        14


Some variables here have missing values, and union in particular has a substantial number. Resist the urge to run na.omit() on the whole dataset. That would drop any woman missing a response on any variable, including ones you are not using, and can silently discard hundreds of cases you had no reason to lose.
lm() handles this for you by dropping incomplete cases on a model-by-model basis. The consequence is that different models in this chapter may be fit on slightly different subsamples, which matters when you compare them. Watch the N in the results tables.

text:
2.2 A single predictor

describe(nlsw$wage)

   vars    n mean   sd median trimmed mad min   max range skew kurtosis   se
X1    1 2246 7.77 5.76   6.27     6.8 3.4   1 40.75 39.74 3.09    12.84 0.12



ggplot(nlsw, aes(x = wage)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1a7a6e", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Hourly Wages",
       x = "Hourly wage (1988 dollars)", y = "Number of women") +
  theme_minimal()



Figure 2.1: Distribution of hourly wages. Note the right skew.



Wages are right-skewed, which is nearly always true of earnings data. A small number of high earners pull the mean above the median. This is worth noticing before modeling, because it affects how well a linear model will describe the data and how much influence those high earners will have on the estimates.

m1 <- lm(wage ~ ttl_exp, data = nlsw)

summary(m1)


Call:
lm(formula = wage ~ ttl_exp, data = nlsw)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-8.502 -2.911 -1.295  1.308 35.370 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  3.61249    0.33935   10.64   <2e-16 ***
ttl_exp      0.33143    0.02541   13.04   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.55 on 2244 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.07048,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.07006 
F-statistic: 170.1 on 1 and 2244 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The coefficient on ttl_exp is the estimated difference in hourly wage associated with one additional year of total work experience.
Three habits of careful interpretation are worth stating explicitly. First, this is an association, not an effect. Causality is a function of research design, not of analysis, and nobody randomly assigned these women to accumulate different amounts of work experience. Second, the intercept is the predicted wage when experience equals zero, which here describes a woman with no work history at all. That is a real if unusual case, so the intercept is at least interpretable. Third, R^2 is the proportion of variance in wages the model accounts for. It is not the probability the model is right, and a model with low R^2 can still contain a coefficient worth knowing about.

title: 2  Review of Regression
section: 2.3 Building up a series of models
text:
2.3 Building up a series of models

m2 <- lm(wage ~ ttl_exp + age, data = nlsw)
m3 <- lm(wage ~ ttl_exp + age + collgrad_f, data = nlsw)

summary(m3)


Call:
lm(formula = wage ~ ttl_exp + age + collgrad_f, data = nlsw)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-9.917 -2.689 -1.021  1.086 35.550 

Coefficients:
                       Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)             7.92690    1.46037   5.428 6.31e-08 ***
ttl_exp                 0.30869    0.02491  12.391  < 2e-16 ***
age                    -0.12252    0.03731  -3.284  0.00104 ** 
collgrad_fCollege grad  3.24134    0.26799  12.095  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.366 on 2242 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.132, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1308 
F-statistic: 113.6 on 3 and 2242 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Watch what happens to the experience coefficient as age and college graduation enter the model. Experience and age are correlated, since older women have had more time to accumulate work history, so some of what the first model attributed to experience was partly age. This is what “controlling for” means in practice, and it is why a coefficient is a statement about a particular model rather than a property of the world.
Notice also how R handles the factor. It picks a reference category, here “Not college grad,” and the coefficient describes the difference from that reference. Had collgrad been a three-category variable left as 1, 2, 3, we would have gotten a single nonsensical slope instead of two comparisons.

title: 2  Review of Regression
text:
2.4 An interaction
Does the return to work experience depend on age?

m4 <- lm(wage ~ ttl_exp * age + collgrad_f, data = nlsw)

summary(m4)


Call:
lm(formula = wage ~ ttl_exp * age + collgrad_f, data = nlsw)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-9.535 -2.646 -1.027  1.064 35.940 

Coefficients:
                        Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)             1.701472   4.151041   0.410   0.6819    
ttl_exp                 0.816992   0.318256   2.567   0.0103 *  
age                     0.034692   0.104979   0.330   0.7411    
collgrad_fCollege grad  3.229193   0.268005  12.049   <2e-16 ***
ttl_exp:age            -0.012788   0.007982  -1.602   0.1093    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.364 on 2241 degrees of freedom

The interaction term asks whether the wage return to an additional year of experience is different for older women than for younger women. When an interaction is present, the main effects are no longer “the effect of experience” in general. They are the effect of experience when age equals zero, which is not a meaningful case here. This is the standard argument for centering continuous predictors before interacting them:

nlsw <- nlsw |>
  mutate(
    age_c     = age - mean(age, na.rm = TRUE),
    ttl_exp_c = ttl_exp - mean(ttl_exp, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

m5 <- lm(wage ~ ttl_exp_c * age_c + collgrad_f, data = nlsw)

summary(m5)

The interaction coefficient is identical in the two models. What changes is the interpretability of everything else. In the centered version, the experience coefficient is the return to experience for a woman of average age, which is a quantity you can put in a sentence.

title: 2  Review of Regression
text:
2.7 Where this breaks
Here is the assumption that does not appear on any of those diagnostic plots: independence of observations. Every standard error above was computed as though these 2,246 women were 2,246 independent pieces of information.
That assumption is often wrong. Women are not scattered randomly across the labor market. They work in particular industries and occupations, which differ in pay scales, unionization, and credential requirements. If two women in the same industry are more alike than two women drawn at random, the independence assumption fails and the standard errors above are too small.
So the natural next question is whether we should be fitting a multilevel model to account for it. Working through that question carefully is the point of this section, and the answer for these data is no.

The mistake to avoid is treating any categorical variable as a potential clustering variable. Grouping structure is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. Start by counting.

That count is the whole problem. A random intercept does not estimate a set of group means. It estimates a variance describing how group means are spread around the overall average, and it does so from as many observations as there are groups. Estimating a variance from a handful of numbers is exactly as unreliable as it sounds. You would not report a standard deviation computed from nine cases and treat it as precise; the variance component here rests on no more information than that.
Common guidance puts the minimum somewhere around 30 to 50 level-2 units for a variance component to be estimated with reasonable precision, with roughly 20 as an absolute floor below which the estimate should not be trusted at all. These data are well below any of those thresholds.

But that industry-level variance was estimated from a single-digit number of industries, and the uncertainty around it is enormous. Confidence intervals make the situation visible:

The interval on the group-level standard deviation is wide, and often runs nearly to zero. That is the model telling you it cannot pin this quantity down. Reporting the point estimate without that interval would imply a precision the data cannot support.






The question is not “are there groups?”



Almost every dataset has categorical variables. Sex, treatment condition, region, program type, marital status. None of those are clustering variables for multilevel modeling, and treating them as such is the single most common error students make when first choosing a model.
Before writing (1 | something), ask three questions:

How many units are there? Fewer than about 20 and the variance component is not estimable with any precision. Between 20 and 50, proceed but report uncertainty honestly. Above 50 you are on solid ground.
Are these units a sample from a larger population you want to generalize to? This is the conceptual heart of it. Random effects treat groups as draws from a population of groups, so that your conclusions extend to schools or classrooms or hospitals you did not observe. The 160 schools in the next chapter are a sample of schools. Nine industries are not a sample of industries; they are the complete set of categories the survey used. There is no broader population of industries you are inferring toward.
Do you want to estimate group-specific effects, or the variation among groups? If you want to know how each category differs, that is a fixed effect. If you want to know how much categories vary as a class, and to generalize beyond the ones you have, that is a random effect.

Sex has two categories. Treatment has two. Neither is a clustering variable, no matter how the data are grouped.



2.8.2 The right tool for a small number of categories
When there are few groups and you have them all, put them in as fixed effects. You get a direct estimate for each category, no variance component to estimate badly, and no implied generalization to unobserved industries.

You can also address the standard error problem directly, without a multilevel model, using cluster-robust standard errors. That approach corrects the inference for within-group correlation while making no attempt to estimate a group-level variance. With few clusters it is generally the safer choice, though it too has small-sample limitations, and Chapter 10 returns to it.

title: 2  Review of Regression
section: 2.9 What these data cannot show us
text:
2.9 What these data cannot show us
nlsw88 is, for our purposes, a single-level dataset. It has grouping variables, but none with enough units to support the models this book is about. That is worth saying plainly rather than forcing a demonstration the data cannot bear.
To see clustering properly modeled we need data with many level-2 units and a genuine sample of them. The next chapter uses 7,185 students nested in 160 schools, which satisfies both conditions comfortably. Those 160 schools are a sample from the population of American high schools, so the between-school variance means something we can generalize.
Two ideas from this chapter carry forward. The first is statistical: treating clustered observations as independent produces standard errors that are too small and p-values that are too optimistic. The second is conceptual and more interesting: a regression using all observations at once blends the comparison between two people in the same group with the comparison between two groups, and returns a single number that is cleanly neither. Multilevel modeling addresses both, provided you have the grouping structure to support it.

title: 3  The Null Model
text:
3.4 Running a null model
The null model, also called the unconditional model or the empty model, has no predictors at all. It only asks how the total variation in math achievement divides into two pieces: variation between schools, and variation among students within the same school.
The (1 | schoolid) term is what makes this a multilevel model. It tells lmer() to estimate a separate intercept for each school, drawn from a distribution whose variance we want to estimate.

model_null <- lmer(mathach ~ 1 + (1 | schoolid), data = hsb, REML = FALSE)

Why REML = FALSE?



lmer() can estimate a model two ways, and the choice affects the variance components you are about to interpret.
Restricted maximum likelihood (REML), the default, produces less biased estimates of variance components, particularly when the number of level-2 units is small. If your goal is to report a variance or an ICC as accurately as possible, REML has the edge.
Maximum likelihood (ML), which REML = FALSE requests, is required whenever you want to compare two models that differ in their fixed effects. REML likelihoods computed under different fixed-effect specifications are not comparable, so an anova() comparison of REML-fitted models with different predictors is not valid. R will usually refit them for you, but silently, and it is better to know why.
This book uses ML throughout, for two reasons. Model comparison happens constantly in these chapters, and using one estimator everywhere means the numbers on one page match the numbers on the next. With 160 schools here, and reasonable numbers of clusters in most course datasets, the difference between ML and REML variance estimates is small.
Where the number of level-2 units is genuinely small, chapter 11 works with just 17 schools, REML is worth considering for the final reported model. Say which you used either way.


Two numbers in the Random effects section carry the story. The variance associated with schoolid is the between-school variance, often written \tau_{00}. The Residual variance is the within-school, student-level variance, written \sigma^2.

title: 3  The Null Model
text:
3.5 Post-estimation: calculating the ICC
The intraclass correlation coefficient is the proportion of total variance that lies between schools:
\text{ICC} = \frac{\tau_{00}}{\tau_{00} + \sigma^2}
It is worth computing this by hand at least once, because the formula is the concept. You can pull the variance components directly out of the fitted model rather than typing them in, which avoids transcription errors:

vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model_null))

tau00 <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "schoolid"]
sigma2 <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "Residual"]

icc_by_hand <- tau00 / (tau00 + sigma2)
icc_by_hand

[1] 0.1793109


The performance package will do the same calculation for you, and you should get the same answer:

performance::icc(model_null)

# Intraclass Correlation Coefficient

    Adjusted ICC: 0.179
  Unadjusted ICC: 0.179


An ICC of roughly this size tells us that a meaningful share of the variation in math achievement is between schools rather than within them. It also tells us something practical: students in the same school are more similar to one another than two students picked at random from the full sample, which is exactly the condition that makes ordinary regression standard errors too small.

text:
3.8 Interpreting the fixed intercept
One last point that students routinely get wrong. The fixed-effect intercept in the null model is not simply the mean of all 7,185 students’ scores. It is an estimate of the average of the school means, weighting schools in a way that accounts for how many students each contributes and how much schools vary. With balanced data the two are close. With unbalanced data they can differ, and the multilevel estimate is usually the quantity you actually want.

4.7 Step five: adding level-two predictors
GTSIG and GLEAD are company averages. Adding them alongside the individual-level versions is not redundancy, even though it looks like it at first glance. These two coefficients answer different questions.
The individual-level coefficient asks: within a given company, do soldiers who report higher task significance report less hostility? A soldier can be high on task significance in a company where everyone is low, or low in a company where everyone is high. Those are different situations, and they can have different consequences.

section: 4.9 What to take from this chapter
text:
4.9 What to take from this chapter
Three ideas are worth carrying forward. Level-one and level-two versions of the same construct answer different questions and belong in the model together. Variance components tell a story as you build models, and watching them shrink is how you know where your predictors are doing work. And an interaction is much easier to defend when you can show someone the plot.
In the next chapter we relax an assumption we have been making all along, that the relationship between a predictor and the outcome is identical in every group.

5.3.1 Reading the singular fit
You will likely see boundary (singular) fit: see ?isSingular, and the random effects table will show an intercept-slope correlation at or very near -1.00.
This is worth stopping on rather than stepping past. A correlation of exactly -1 is not a finding about the Army. It is the model telling you it has run out of information. The estimation has pushed a parameter to the edge of the space it is allowed to occupy, which is what happens when 49 companies cannot support an intercept variance, a slope variance, and a correlation among them all at once.
The practical question is what to do about it. A singular fit does not invalidate the fixed effects, which are usually what you are reporting. It does mean the random effects structure should be treated with suspicion, and it is a reason to consider dropping the correlation:

The likelihood ratio test gives you statistical evidence. It should not be the only thing you consult. A random slope that improves fit but has no substantive rationale is worth questioning, and a slope with a strong theoretical rationale that narrowly misses significance may still deserve to stay, particularly with a modest number of level-2 units.
Note also what a significant result here means. Testing whether a variance equals zero puts the null hypothesis on the boundary of the parameter space, which makes the usual chi-square reference distribution conservative. A significant result is therefore trustworthy; a marginal one deserves more caution than the p-value suggests.

5.6 A cross-level interaction
This is more advanced, but worth showing. In the previous chapter we looked at an interaction between LEAD and TSIG, both level-1 soldier covariates. Multilevel models also let us test cross-level interactions, between a level-1 and a level-2 predictor.
Suppose we want to test an interaction between TSIG (level 1) and GTSIG (level 2). Put another way: is there an interaction between how I feel about the importance of my job, and how my peers feel about the importance of theirs? That seems worth testing.

5.6.1 Center the predictors first
Centering means subtracting the mean from every observation, so that zero now means average. When examining interactions it is usually a good idea to center continuous predictors first. This makes the results easier to interpret, and it ensures the interaction is evaluated near the sample mean rather than at a value that may not exist in the data.

  mutate(

    gtsig_cent = GTSIG - mean(GTSIG)

text:
6.2 Proportional reduction in variance
The most interpretable multilevel effect sizes ask how much variance a model explains relative to the null model, computed separately at each level. Extract the variance components first:

vc_null <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_null))
vc_cond <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_cond))

tau_null   <- vc_null$vcov[vc_null$grp == "strs3"]
sigma_null <- vc_null$vcov[vc_null$grp == "Residual"]

tau_cond   <- vc_cond$vcov[vc_cond$grp == "strs3"]
sigma_cond <- vc_cond$vcov[vc_cond$grp == "Residual"]

c(tau_null = tau_null, sigma_null = sigma_null,
  tau_cond = tau_cond, sigma_cond = sigma_cond)

  tau_null sigma_null   tau_cond sigma_cond 
 0.7675085  0.1325110  0.5055268  0.1051911 


Within-group proportional reduction in variance is the share of student-level variance the predictors account for:

wg_prv <- (sigma_null - sigma_cond) / sigma_null
wg_prv

[1] 0.2061703


Between-group PRV does the same at the teacher level:

bg_prv <- (tau_null - tau_cond) / tau_null
bg_prv

[1] 0.3413405


And a total, or multilevel, R^2 uses the combined variance:

total_null <- tau_null + sigma_null
total_cond <- tau_cond + sigma_cond

ml_r2 <- (total_null - total_cond) / total_null
ml_r2

[1] 0.3214393


Be precise about what each denominator refers to when you write these up. WG-PRV is the proportion of student-level variance explained, not the proportion of all variance. Reporting it as though it were an overall R^2 overstates your model considerably.

6.2.1 When PRV comes out negative
A negative PRV looks like an arithmetic mistake and usually is not. Adding a level-one predictor can increase the estimated level-two variance, because the level-two variance is estimated conditional on everything else in the model. If a student-level predictor is unevenly distributed across teachers, controlling for it can reveal teacher differences that were previously masked. Report the negative value and explain it. Deleting it from your table is the one clearly wrong response.

This reports marginal R^2, the variance explained by fixed effects alone, and conditional R^2, the variance explained by fixed and random effects together. These are Nakagawa’s measures, and they answer a slightly different question than the PRV statistics above. Both are defensible. Say which you used.

6.5.1 When the criteria disagree
They often will, and understanding why is more useful than memorizing a rule. AIC and BIC both penalize complexity, but BIC’s penalty grows with sample size while AIC’s does not. With a large sample, BIC prefers simpler models more aggressively than AIC does. The likelihood ratio test is a third thing again: a hypothesis test with a null of no improvement, which inherits all the usual sensitivities to sample size.
For random effects there is an additional wrinkle. Testing whether a variance component equals zero puts the null on the boundary of the parameter space, which makes the usual chi-square reference distribution conservative. The ranova() function handles this, but it is a reason not to treat a p-value of .06 on a variance component as decisive.
When the criteria disagree, say so, state which you weighted and why, and check whether your substantive conclusions change between the two models. If the treatment effect is essentially identical either way, the model choice matters less than it appears to.

section: 6.6 When a model will not converge
text:
6.6 When a model will not converge
Ask for two random slopes and the data may refuse:

m_two_slopes <- lmer(conflict_post ~ treat + conflict_pre_c + closeness_pre_c +
                       (1 + conflict_pre_c + closeness_pre_c | strs3),
                     data = strs, REML = FALSE)

Error: number of observations (=828) <= number of random effects (=966) for term (1 + conflict_pre_c + closeness_pre_c | strs3); the random-effects parameters and the residual variance (or scale parameter) are probably unidentifiable


This one does not merely warn. It refuses to fit at all, and the error message tells you exactly why. Asking for an intercept and two slopes for each of 322 teachers means asking for 966 random effects, and we have only 828 observations. There are more quantities to estimate than there are data points to estimate them from, so the model is unidentifiable.
It is worth doing that arithmetic yourself before fitting a complex random effects structure. Multiply the number of level-two units by the number of random effects you are requesting per unit, and compare it to your sample size. If the first number approaches the second, the model is in trouble whether or not R throws an error.
The more common situation is milder. Instead of an outright refusal you get a singular fit, a variance component estimated at essentially zero, or a correlation of exactly 1 or -1. Those are the same message delivered more politely. The data cannot support that many random effects.
The usual responses, in order of how much you give up: drop the correlations and keep both slopes uncorrelated; drop the less theoretically important slope; or return to a random intercept model and acknowledge in your write-up that slope variation could not be estimated with these data. All three are defensible. Silently reporting a singular model as though nothing happened is not.

# Uncorrelated random effects
m_uncorr <- lmer(conflict_post ~ treat + conflict_pre_c + closeness_pre_c +
                   (1 | strs3) + (0 + conflict_pre_c | strs3),
                 data = strs, REML = FALSE)

7.3 What ignoring a level costs you
Suppose we had modeled only students within schools, ignoring classrooms entirely.

m_null2 <- lmer(gktmathss ~ 1 + (1 | gkschid), data = star, REML = FALSE)

vc2 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_null2))
vc2

       grp        var1 var2      vcov    sdcor
1  gkschid (Intercept) <NA>  450.7584 21.23107
2 Residual        <NA> <NA> 1826.3914 42.73630


Compare the school-level variance in this model to the one in the three-level model. Dropping the classroom level does not make classroom variation disappear. It redistributes it, and much of it lands at whichever level remains. A researcher looking only at the two-level model would conclude that schools matter more than they do, when part of what they are seeing is teachers.

A note on the school mean. Computing a group average from the same outcome you are predicting and then using it as a predictor is common practice, but it deserves care. The school mean is partly composed of the very students whose scores you are modeling, which builds in a mechanical relationship. With large schools the contribution of any one student is small and the practice is generally accepted. With small clusters it can be seriously misleading.






About convergence warnings



Models this complex frequently produce singularity or convergence warnings. For these data the model still converges and returns usable estimates and standard errors. Do not ignore such warnings by reflex, but do read them as diagnostic information rather than as a verdict. A singular fit usually means one variance component is being estimated at or near zero.

title: 8  Longitudinal and Growth Curve Models
text:
8.1 Coding time
Almost always, code time so that zero is a meaningful moment. Here grade runs 3 to 8, so we subtract 3 and get a variable running 0 to 5.

star_long <- star_long |>
  mutate(grade_0 = grade - 3)

This is not cosmetic. The intercept in a growth model is the predicted outcome when every predictor equals zero, including time. Left as 3 through 8, the intercept would describe a hypothetical student in grade zero, extrapolated three years before anyone was measured. Centered at the first wave, the intercept becomes the predicted score at the study’s start, which is a quantity you can defend in print.

Compare the residual variance across the two models. It drops substantially once time is in the model, and the reason is worth stating carefully. In the first model, “within-student variance” lumps together everything that makes a student’s six scores differ, including the fact that they are growing. text:
8.8 Heterogeneous variance structures
Standard multilevel models assume the level-one residual variance is constant across occasions. That assumption is often wrong for longitudinal data, where scores tend to spread out as children develop. The nlme package can relax it.

library(nlme)

m_homog <- lme(science ~ grade0 + grade0_sq,
               random = ~ 1 | stdntid,
               data = star_clean, method = "ML",
               na.action = na.omit)

m_heterog <- lme(science ~ grade0 + grade0_sq,
                 random = ~ 1 | stdntid,
                 weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | grade0),
                 data = star_clean, method = "ML",
                 na.action = na.omit)

text:
9.2 The ICC, with a wrinkle
In a linear model we computed the ICC from two estimated variances. In a logistic model there is no estimated level-one variance, because for a binary outcome the residual variance is determined by the mean. The standard solution fixes it at \pi^2/3 \approx 3.29, the variance of the standard logistic distribution:
\text{ICC} = \frac{\tau_{00}}{\tau_{00} + \pi^2/3}

vc <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m_null))
tau00 <- vc$vcov[vc$grp == "school_id"]

icc_logistic <- tau00 / (tau00 + (pi^2 / 3))

Because that level-one variance is assumed rather than estimated, the logistic ICC is on a latent scale and is not directly comparable to an ICC from a linear model. Treat it as a rough indication of clustering, not as a precise proportion of variance in the observed outcome.

9.3.1 Saying it correctly
An odds ratio of 2.4 for peer inclusivity means the odds of reporting strong belonging are 2.4 times higher for students who perceive their peers as inclusive, holding the other predictors constant and comparing students within the same school.
It does not mean those students are 2.4 times more likely to feel belonging. Odds and probability are different quantities, and they diverge sharply when outcomes are common. If the baseline probability is 50 percent, an odds ratio of 2.4 corresponds to about 71 percent, not 120 percent, which would be impossible. The looser phrasing is only approximately right when the outcome is rare, and it is worth avoiding entirely.

10.2 Normality of residuals

ggplot(aug, aes(x = std_resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#1a7a6e", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Standardized Residuals", x = "Standardized residual", y = "Count") +

  stat_qq(alpha = 0.3, color = "#1a7a6e") +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#b2182b") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot", x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles") +
  theme_minimal()



Figure 10.2: Normal Q-Q plot of standardized residuals.




10.2.1 How many observations are we actually working with?
Before running a formal test, check how large the analysis sample is. This is not the same as the number of rows in the file:

nrow(star)      # rows in the dataset

[1] 6325

nrow(aug)       # rows the model actually used

[1] 4756


Those two numbers differ, sometimes substantially. lmer() drops any case missing a value on the outcome or on any predictor, a behavior called listwise deletion, and it does so silently. Adding one predictor with a lot of missingness can shrink your analysis sample dramatically without any warning appearing.
This matters for more than the diagnostics below. If you compare two models fit on different subsamples, the comparison is not valid, which is why the N row in a results table is worth reading rather than skipping. It is also the reason to check missingness before modeling rather than after.

10.2.2 A formal test, with a caveat

# Shapiro-Wilk accepts between 3 and 5,000 observations, so sample if needed
if (nrow(aug) > 5000) {
  set.seed(664)
  shapiro.test(sample(aug$std_resid, 5000))
} else {
  shapiro.test(aug$std_resid)
}


    Shapiro-Wilk normality test

data:  aug$std_resid
W = 0.99119, p-value < 2.2e-16


Expect this to be significant, and do not make much of it. Shapiro-Wilk detects arbitrarily small departures from normality once the sample is reasonably large, and at these sample sizes it will reject for essentially any real dataset. The histogram and Q-Q plot carry the information here. What you are looking for is severe skew, heavy tails, or obvious multimodality, not a p-value.
It is also worth remembering what this assumption buys. Normality of residuals matters for small-sample inference. With samples this size, the central limit theorem does most of the work regardless.

A fan or funnel suggests the residual variance depends on the fitted value. A silent failure worth knowing about



Writing gktchid = names(cooks) looks reasonable and is wrong here, because cooks.distance() on an influence.ME object returns a matrix whose labels live in rownames(). names() on that matrix returns NULL.
The dangerous part is what happens next. tibble() drops NULL columns without complaint, so you get a one-column data frame and no error. Everything that uses only cooks_d keeps working, including the plot below. The failure surfaces later, at the first line that asks for gktchid, which may be several chunks away from the line that actually caused it.
When a variable goes missing without explanation, look upstream for the place it was created, not at the line that reported the error. Running str() on an unfamiliar object before you build a data frame from it costs a second and prevents this whole category of problem.

A classroom that is simply unusual, small and high-achieving, is data. Deleting inconvenient observations because a statistic flagged them is not a diagnostic procedure, it is a way of guaranteeing the result you already wanted.

The obvious thing to write is coef_test(m, vcov = "CR2", cluster = star$gktchid), and it fails with arguments must have same length.
The reason is the listwise deletion we looked at earlier in this chapter. star$gktchid has one entry per row of the dataset, while the model was fit on the smaller set of complete cases. The two vectors do not line up, and clubSandwich cannot tell which classroom each residual belongs to.

title: 10  Assessing Assumptions
text:
10.6 Writing it up
A sensitivity analysis paragraph belongs in nearly every quantitative paper, and it has a predictable shape. State which diagnostics you examined. Report what they showed, honestly, including the parts that looked imperfect. Describe the robustness checks you ran. Then state whether your substantive conclusion held.
The version that reads as defensive says the assumptions were met and moves on. The version that reads as competent concedes that residuals showed mild right skew and 14 classrooms exceeded the conventional Cook’s distance threshold, then reports that the class size estimate changed by less than a tenth of a point under cluster-robust standard errors and with those classrooms excluded. The second version is more honest and considerably more persuasive.

title: 11  Cross-Classified Models
text:
11.4 Why the variances shift
Compare the school variance in m_school to the school variance in m_cross, and do the same for neighborhoods. Both typically shrink when the two factors are modeled together.
The reason is that a single-factor model has nowhere to put the other source of variation. When you fit schools alone, any neighborhood differences get absorbed into the school variance, because students in the same school tend to come from overlapping neighborhoods. The school-only model attributes to schools some variation that actually belongs to where children live. Fitting both simultaneously lets each factor account for its own share.
This has a direct bearing on school accountability research. A model that ignores neighborhoods will systematically overstate how much schools matter.

  summarize(

    n_neighborhoods = n_distinct(neighid),

With only 17 schools, the school-level variance is estimated from very little information. Variance components need a reasonable number of higher-level units to be estimated precisely, and common rules of thumb suggest wanting at least 30 to 50. The neighborhood variance, resting on 500-plus units, is on much firmer ground.
This asymmetry should shape how you write up the results. Report both variances, but attach appropriate uncertainty to claims about schools. A school-level variance that appears smaller than the neighborhood variance may reflect a genuine difference, or it may reflect that 17 units cannot pin down a variance with much precision.

title: 11  Cross-Classified Models
text:
11.9 Recognizing this structure elsewhere
Cross-classification is more common than it looks once you start watching for it. Students crossed with teachers across multiple years. Patients crossed with hospitals and with surgeons who operate at several hospitals. Employees crossed with firms and with occupations. Survey respondents crossed with interviewers and with geographic areas.
The diagnostic question is simple. Does every unit in group A belong to exactly one unit in group B? If yes, the structure is nested. If units in A spread across multiple units in B, it is crossed, and modeling it as nested will misattribute variance between the two.
